title: Sets, Relations, and Functions
intro: From set notation to Warshall's algorithm and inverse functions, with worked examples.

sec.s: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects.

b.x: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The objects are called elements or members. For example, A = {1, 2, 3} is a set containing three elements. The phrase “well-defined” means that it must be possible to decide whether a given object belongs to the collection.
Notation

x: x ∈ A means x is an element of A.
x ∉ A means x is not an element of A.
A = B means A and B contain exactly the same elements.
∅ denotes the empty set, which has no elements.
U often denotes a universal set: the collection of all objects under discussion.

b.x: Order and repetition do not matter in ordinary sets. Thus {1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 1} and {1, 1, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3}. This differs from lists and arrays in programming, where order and repeated entries may matter.
Ways to describe a set

x: Roster form: list elements, e.g. A = {2, 4, 6, 8}.
Set-builder form: state a property, e.g. A = {x ∈ Z | x is even and 2 ≤ x ≤ 8}.
Descriptive form: “the set of vowels in English,” often written {a, e, i, o, u}.

b.x: Common number sets

x: N: natural numbers; convention varies on whether 0 is included, so a course should state its convention.
Q: rational numbers, expressible as p/q where p, q ∈ Z and q ≠ 0.

b.x: Finite and infinite sets

A finite set has a limited number of elements, such as {a, b, c}. An infinite set has infinitely many elements, such as Z. The cardinality of a finite set A, written |A| or n(A), is its number of elements. For example, if A = {red, blue, green}, then |A| = 3.

Disjoint sets have no common elements: A ∩ B = ∅. Overlapping sets share at least one element. The universal set depends on context: when discussing students in one class, U might be all students in that class, not every person in the world.

x: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. Then 2 ∈ A, 5 ∉ A, and A ≠ B because A contains 1 and 2 while B does not.

sec.s: Set operations create new sets from existing ones.

b.x: Set operations create new sets from existing ones.
2.1 Union

x: The union of A and B contains every element that belongs to A or B or both:
A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
In logic, union corresponds to inclusive OR.

b.x: 2.2 Intersection

x: The intersection contains only elements common to both sets:
A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
For the same A and B, A ∩ B = {3}. Intersection corresponds to AND.

b.x: 2.3 Difference

x: The difference A − B (also written A \\ B) contains elements in A that are not in B:
A − B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
A − B = {1, 2}, while B − A = {4, 5}. Difference is generally not commutative: A − B need not equal B − A.

Relative to universal set U, the complement of A is

x: If U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and A = {1, 3, 5}, then Aᶜ = {2, 4, 6}. A complement cannot be specified unambiguously without knowing U.

b.x: 2.5 Symmetric difference
A △ B consists of elements in exactly one of A and B

For any x

x: x ∈ A ∪ B exactly when x ∈ A or x ∈ B.
x ∈ A ∩ B exactly when x ∈ A and x ∈ B.
x ∈ A − B exactly when x ∈ A and x ∉ B.

sec.s: A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B, if every element of A is also in B:

b.x: A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B, if every element of A is also in B:
A ⊆ B iff for every x, x ∈ A implies x ∈ B.
For example, {1,2} ⊆ {1,2,3}. A is a proper subset of B, written A ⊊ B, if A ⊆ B but A ≠ B.
Important facts

x: Every set is a subset of itself: A ⊆ A.
The empty set is a subset of every set: ∅ ⊆ A.
If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A, then A = B.
A ⊆ B does not necessarily mean B ⊆ A.

b.x: Do not confuse “element of” and “subset of.” If A = {1,2}, then 1 ∈ A, but {1} ⊆ A. The expression {1} ∈ A is false for this example because the elements of A are 1 and 2, not the set {1}.

sec.s: A Venn diagram represents sets as closed regions, usually circles, inside a rectangle representing the…

b.x: A Venn diagram represents sets as closed regions, usually circles, inside a rectangle representing the universal set. Overlapping areas represent shared membership.
For two sets

x: Outside A but inside U: Aᶜ.

b.x: To shade A − B, shade the part of A that lies outside B. To shade (A ∪ B)ᶜ, shade everything in the universal rectangle outside both A and B. To shade A ∩ B, shade only the overlap.

Venn diagrams help visualize identities, but a diagram is not always a complete proof for arbitrary sets; the element-by-element method is more formal. For three sets, three circles can show individual-only regions, pairwise overlaps, and the triple intersection.

x: Suppose 40 students are surveyed; 22 like web development, 18 like AI, and 10 like both. Then 22 − 10 = 12 like only web development, 18 − 10 = 8 like only AI, and 22 + 18 − 10 = 30 like at least one. The remaining 10 like neither.

sec.s: Order matters: generally (a,b) ≠ (b,a).

x: The Cartesian product of A and B is the set of ordered pairs:
A × B = {(a,b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}.

b.x: Order matters: generally (a,b) ≠ (b,a). Consequently, A × B generally differs from B × A. For example, (1,x) belongs to A × B, but it is not an element of B × A because its first component is not in B.
The Cartesian square A² means A × A. If A = {0,1}, then A² = {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)}.
Applications

x: A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.
A database table can be understood as a collection of records with fields.
A grid of coordinates uses ordered pairs.
Testing every pair in A × A is a straightforward way to inspect a relation on a finite set.

b.x: For three sets, A × B × C contains ordered triples (a,b,c), and its finite cardinality is |A||B||C|.

sec.s: The inverse relation is R⁻¹ = {(b,a) | (a,b) ∈ R}.

b.x: A binary relation R from A to B is any subset of A × B

x: If A = B, R is called a relation on A. If (a,b) ∈ R, we may write a R b, read “a is related to b.”
The domain of R is the set of first components that actually occur: {1,2}.
The range of R is the set of second components that actually occur: {a,b}.
The codomain is B, which in this example is also {a,b}. In other examples, the range may be smaller than the codomain.

b.x: A relation can be described by

x: A rule, such as x R y iff x ≤ y.

b.x: Example on A = {1,2,3}: define x R y iff x divides y. Then

x: Because 1 divides every positive integer, pairs beginning with 1 occur. The relation is defined only over the chosen set A, so the pairs are restricted to A × A.

b.x: The inverse relation is R⁻¹ = {(b,a) | (a,b) ∈ R}. If R represents “is a prerequisite of,” the inverse represents “has as a prerequisite” under the corresponding interpretation.

Composition of relations can also be defined: if R ⊆ A × B and S ⊆ B × C, then S ∘ R contains (a,c) when there is some b ∈ B such that (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S. This is related to paths of length two in a graph.

sec.s: Let R be a relation on a set A.

b.x: Let R be a relation on a set A.
8.1 Reflexive
R is reflexive if every element is related to itself

x: ≤ on integers is reflexive because a ≤ a. A relation containing (1,1) and (2,2) but not (3,3) is not reflexive on {1,2,3}.

b.x: 8.2 Irreflexive
R is irreflexive if no element is related to itself

x: < on integers is irreflexive because no integer is less than itself.
“Irreflexive” is stronger than merely “not reflexive.” A relation may contain some but not all self-pairs and therefore be neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

b.x: 8.3 Symmetric
R is symmetric if a R b implies b R a

x: For all a,b ∈ A, (a,b) ∈ R ⇒ (b,a) ∈ R.
“has the same age as” is symmetric. “is less than” is not symmetric.

b.x: 8.4 Antisymmetric

x: R is antisymmetric if a R b and b R a together imply a = b.
For all a,b ∈ A, [(a,b) ∈ R and (b,a) ∈ R] ⇒ a = b.
The usual ≤ relation is antisymmetric: if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b.
Antisymmetric does not mean “not symmetric.” A relation can be both symmetric and antisymmetric, for example equality.

b.x: 8.5 Asymmetric
R is asymmetric if a R b implies that b R a is false. An asymmetric relation is necessarily irreflexive. The relation < is asymmetric.
8.6 Transitive
R is transitive if a R b and b R c imply a R c

x: if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c. “Is a biological sibling of” is not always safely transitive in every real-world definition; mathematical examples should be chosen with care.

b.x: 8.7 Total/connected relation

A relation R on A is often called total or connected (terminology varies) if for every distinct a,b ∈ A, at least one of a R b or b R a holds. The usual order ≤ on numbers has this property. A partial order need not compare every pair.
How to test a finite relation

x: Irreflexive: check that no diagonal pair exists.
Antisymmetric: look for distinct a,b with both directions present.
Transitive: for every two-step chain a R b and b R c, check that a R c is present.

It is reflexive. It is symmetric because (1,2) and (2,1) both appear. It is not antisymmetric because 1 ≠ 2 but both directions appear. It is transitive: the only nontrivial two-way links among 1 and 2 are completed by the diagonal pairs; 3 is related only to itself. Hence R is an equivalence relation.

b.x: 9.2 Digraph representation

A directed graph has vertices for set elements and arrows for relation pairs. A loop at a vertex represents (a,a). An arrow a → b represents (a,b) ∈ R. If both a → b and b → a appear, the relation includes both ordered pairs.
For the previous relation, draw vertices 1, 2, 3; add loops only if the diagonal pairs exist, and add arrows 1 → 2, 2 → 3, and 3 → 1. A digraph can make cycles and reachability visually obvious.
Matrix versus digraph

x: Matrices are convenient for algorithmic processing and systematic checking.
Digraphs are often easier for visualizing structure, loops, paths, and cycles.
Both represent the same information if the vertex order is fixed.

sec.s: Common named types include:

b.x: Common named types include:

x: Empty relation: R = ∅. No pair is related. On a nonempty set, it is irreflexive and symmetric, but not reflexive.
Universal relation: R = A × A. Every element is related to every element. It is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, but is antisymmetric only when A has at most one element.
Identity relation: I_A = {(a,a) | a ∈ A}. It relates every element only to itself. It is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive.
Reflexive relation: contains all diagonal pairs.
Symmetric relation: every pair has its reverse.
Antisymmetric relation: mutual relatedness forces equality.
Transitive relation: two consecutive links imply the direct link.
Equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Partial order: reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
Total order: a partial order in which every pair of elements is comparable.

b.x: Examples

x: Equality (=) is an equivalence relation and a partial order.
Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation.
Subset inclusion ⊆ on a power set is a partial order.
The usual ≤ on integers is a total order.
“is a friend of” may be modeled as symmetric if friendship is treated mutually, but real-world relationships can be ambiguous and may not be transitive.

b.x: A relation may have several properties at once. For instance, equality is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive. Do not assume properties are mutually exclusive.

sec.s: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

b.x: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. These three properties make the relation behave like a generalized notion of equality: elements need not be identical, but they are treated as equivalent under a chosen criterion.

x: For an equivalence relation R on A, the equivalence class of a ∈ A is:
Some books use x R a or a R x; for equivalence relations these give the same class because the relation is symmetric.
Let A = Z and define a R b iff 3 divides (a − b). Then a and b are related if they have the same remainder when divided by 3.
• Symmetric: if 3 divides a − b, then it divides b − a because b − a = −(a − b).
• Transitive: if 3 divides a − b and b − c, it divides their sum a − c.
These classes group integers by remainder.

If A is a set of people and a R b means “a and b have the same age in completed years,” then the relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, assuming ages are measured consistently. Equivalence classes group people by age.

b.x: Important properties of equivalence classes

x: Every element a belongs to its own class [a].
If a is not related to b, then [a] and [b] are disjoint.
Every element of A belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

b.x: Thus equivalence classes divide a set into non-overlapping groups.

sec.s: A partition of a set A is a collection of nonempty subsets of A such that:

b.x: A partition of a set A is a collection of nonempty subsets of A such that:

x: The union of all blocks is A.
A partition is {{1,3,5},{2,4,6}}. The two blocks are nonempty, disjoint, and together cover A.

The collection {{1,2},{2,3},{4,5,6}} is not a partition because the first two blocks overlap at 2 and element 3? More precisely, they overlap at 2 only if both include 2; here {2,3} contains 2, so they overlap, and therefore fail the disjointness requirement.

b.x: There is a fundamental correspondence

x: Every equivalence relation on A produces a partition into equivalence classes.
Every partition of A defines an equivalence relation: a R b iff a and b lie in the same block.
Define a R b when a and b are in the same block. Then:
This relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

Equivalence relations formalize classification. A database can group records by category; a compiler can treat equivalent expressions as interchangeable under rules; modular arithmetic groups integers by remainders. The partition is the group structure, while the relation is the rule for deciding which elements belong together.

b.x: The closure of a relation is the smallest relation containing the original relation and satisfying a desired property. “Smallest” means that no unnecessary ordered pairs are added.
13.1 Reflexive closure
For relation R on A, the reflexive closure is

x: This adds any missing diagonal pairs. It does not remove any existing pairs.

b.x: 13.2 Symmetric closure
The symmetric closure is

x: For every (a,b), it ensures that (b,a) is also present.
It does not automatically make the relation reflexive or transitive.

b.x: 13.3 Transitive closure

The transitive closure is the smallest transitive relation containing R. It adds pairs required by paths. If (a,b) and (b,c) are in the relation, then (a,c) must be included. This requirement may create further required pairs.

For a finite set, think of R as a directed graph. The transitive closure relates a to b whenever there is a directed path from a to b of positive length. Some conventions distinguish reachability by a path of length zero; the usual relation transitive closure for positive-length paths does not automatically add every self-pair. If a vertex lies on a directed cycle, however, a self-pair may be added.

x: Because 1 → 2 and 2 → 3, add (1,3). The transitive closure is {(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)}.

b.x: Closures are not generally interchangeable. A reflexive closure adds loops, symmetric closure adds reverse arrows, and transitive closure adds shortcut arrows for paths. Applying one closure can create situations that require further pairs for another property. If several properties are required simultaneously, the relation may need repeated additions until all requirements hold.

sec.s: Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure of a finite relation using its Boolean adjacency matrix.

b.x: Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure of a finite relation using its Boolean adjacency matrix. It answers a reachability question: can vertex i reach vertex j through one or more directed edges?

In words, i can reach j after allowing vertex k if either the route already existed, or i can reach k and k can reach j.

When k = 1, no new reachability is discovered through vertex 1.

b.x: Complexity

The algorithm has three nested loops, so its time complexity is O(n³). The matrix requires O(n²) space. This is practical for many small and medium-sized dense graphs and is a classic dynamic-programming-style algorithm.

x: • Warshall's algorithm uses Boolean OR/AND, not ordinary arithmetic multiplication.
• It computes reachability/transitive closure, not shortest paths. Floyd–Warshall is a related but different algorithm for shortest paths using distances and minimum-plus updates.

• Whether diagonal entries become 1 depends on whether a positive-length cycle returns to the same vertex. If you want reflexive reachability that includes zero-length paths, initialize the diagonal to 1 before running the algorithm.

sec.s: The defining rule is “exactly one output per input.” Different inputs may produce the same output.

b.x: The defining rule is “exactly one output per input.” Different inputs may produce the same output. An input cannot be assigned two different outputs by the same function.

sec.s: A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

b.x: 17.1 Injective (one-to-one)

x: A function f: A → B is injective if different inputs always have different outputs:
Equivalent wording: no two distinct domain elements map to the same output.
f(x)=2x+1 from R to R is injective. If 2a+1=2b+1, then 2a=2b and a=b.
The function f(x)=x² from R to R is not injective because f(2)=4 and f(−2)=4 while 2 ≠ −2.
However, x² restricted to [0,∞) is injective.

b.x: 17.2 Surjective (onto)

x: A function f: A → B is surjective if every element of the codomain is reached:
For every b ∈ B, there exists a ∈ A such that f(a)=b.
f(x)=x³ from R to R is surjective because every real y has the real preimage x=∛y.
The function f(x)=x² from R to R is not surjective because negative real numbers are not outputs.
But f: R → [0,∞), f(x)=x², is surjective because every nonnegative y has preimage √y (and also −√y when y > 0).

b.x: 17.3 Bijective
A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective. Every codomain element is reached exactly once. For example, f: R → R defined by f(x)=x+4 is bijective.

x: The formula alone does not decide surjectivity; the stated codomain matters. f(x)=x² is not onto R, but it is onto [0,∞) if its domain is R. Always inspect both domain and codomain.

b.x: Finite-set counting

If A and B are finite and have the same number of elements, an injective function A → B is automatically surjective, and a surjective function A → B is automatically injective. If the sizes differ, these conclusions do not generally hold.
Quick tests

x: Injective: suppose f(a)=f(b), then try to prove a=b.
Surjective: take an arbitrary y in the codomain and solve f(x)=y; show a valid x in the domain exists for every y.

The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y=x. This is because the ordered pair (a,b) on f becomes (b,a) on the inverse.

x: where the coefficients aᵢ are real numbers (or another specified field), exponents are nonnegative integers, and the leading coefficient aₙ is nonzero for a nonzero polynomial.

b.x: The degree is the largest exponent with a nonzero coefficient. The leading coefficient is the coefficient of the highest-degree term.
Examples

x: Not a polynomial: 1/x = x⁻¹, because it has a negative exponent.
Not a polynomial: √x = x^(1/2), because the exponent is not a nonnegative integer.

b.x: A polynomial is defined for every real x, so its real domain is R. Its range depends on the polynomial. A nonconstant linear function has range R. A quadratic with positive leading coefficient has a minimum; one with negative leading coefficient has a maximum. For example, f(x)=x² has range [0,∞).

Zeros or roots are values r such that f(r)=0. For f(x)=x²−4x+3=(x−1)(x−3), the roots are 1 and 3. The graph crosses or touches the x-axis at real roots, depending on their multiplicity and local behavior.
End behavior

For large |x|, the leading term usually dominates. If degree is even, both ends of the graph point in the same vertical direction; if degree is odd, the ends point in opposite directions. The leading coefficient determines whether the right-hand end rises or falls.
Polynomial operations

Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The degree of a product of two nonzero polynomials is the sum of their degrees. Division may produce a remainder or a rational expression, so polynomials are not generally closed under division.

Applications include modeling simple trends, representing algebraic relationships, approximating functions, and constructing curves in graphics. Polynomial behavior is also foundational in numerical methods and machine learning feature transformations.

sec.s: The floor function, written floor(x) or ⌊x⌋, is the greatest integer less than or equal to x.

b.x: The floor function, written floor(x) or ⌊x⌋, is the greatest integer less than or equal to x.
The ceiling function, written ceil(x) or ⌈x⌉, is the least integer greater than or equal to x.
Examples

x: Negative examples are important: floor rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero. Ceiling rounds toward positive infinity.

b.x: For every real x
For integer n, ⌊x⌋ = n exactly when n ≤ x < n+1. Also, ⌈x⌉ = n exactly when n−1 < x ≤ n.
Examples

x: A bus carries 40 people per trip. For 101 people, the number of full-capacity trips needed is ⌈101/40⌉ = 3.
If 101 items are stored in boxes holding 40 each, 2 full boxes contain 80 and the remaining 21 go in a third box.
In binary search, the number of times a search interval can be halved is related to logarithms and integer floor/ceiling operations.
Array indexing, chunking records into pages, and integer division often require careful rounding rules.

b.x: Do not assume ⌊x+y⌋ = ⌊x⌋+⌊y⌋; this is not always true. For example, ⌊0.6+0.6⌋=1 while ⌊0.6⌋+⌊0.6⌋=0.

sec.s: A set models a collection of unique items, such as unique user IDs or supported file types.

b.x: Sets

A set models a collection of unique items, such as unique user IDs or supported file types. Set union and intersection can describe combining or filtering groups. Programming languages often provide set data structures, though their exact ordering behavior varies.
Relations

A relation models connections between items. In databases, a relation is also a formal concept associated with a table, though practical SQL tables have implementation details beyond elementary set theory. A prerequisite graph, follower graph, or dependency graph can be modeled as a relation. Relation matrices are adjacency matrices for directed graphs.
Equivalence

Equivalence classes appear in grouping and deduplication. For example, strings can be grouped by lowercase form if the equivalence rule says two strings are equivalent when their lowercase versions match. Care is needed to ensure the chosen rule really is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Functions

Functions are central to programs because a function maps inputs to outputs. Injectivity can matter when unique keys are needed. Surjectivity concerns whether all allowed target values are reachable. Bijective mappings can be reversed without ambiguity.
Closures and reachability

Transitive closure can answer “is there any dependency path from task A to task B?” or “can this node reach that node?” Warshall's algorithm provides a systematic way to compute this for finite graphs.
Exponential and logarithmic functions
Exponential models describe repeated percentage growth or decay. Logarithms measure the number of repeated doubling/halving steps and appear in complexity analysis.
Floor and ceiling
These functions help turn continuous calculations into integer counts. For example, a delivery service needing one van per group of at most k parcels uses a ceiling calculation.

No, because 2 and 3 map to the same output b.
Is f(x)=x+5 from R to R bijective?
Yes. It is injective and every real y has preimage x=y−5.
Find the inverse of f(x)=4x−8 on R.
Set y=4x−8, solve x=(y+8)/4, so f⁻¹(x)=(x+8)/4.

What is the key difference between codomain and range?
The codomain is the declared target set; the range contains only outputs actually attained.
Does a relation have to be a function?
No. A relation can assign one input to multiple outputs or none; a function assigns each domain input exactly one output.

First learn set notation and operations. Then practise relation properties on small sets and write the same relation as ordered pairs, a matrix, and a digraph. Next master equivalence relations and closures, then implement Warshall's algorithm by hand on a 3×3 matrix. Finally practise function types and inverse functions, paying close attention to domain and codomain. For exponential, logarithmic, polynomial, floor, and ceiling functions, always identify the domain and range and evaluate several examples, including negative and boundary values.
